text: In 1902, the city of Hanoi had a serious problem.
Their brand new, modern sewer system was completely overrun with rats.
Officials devised what seemed like a foolproof plan, a bounty,
turn in a rat's tail, collect a payment.
The entire system rested on one basic logical assumption,
one severed tail, then one dead rat.
At first, the program looked like a triumph.
Tails poured in by the thousands, and the payouts flowed.
But measuring success purely by the numbers on a ledger
blinded officials to what was actually happening on the streets.
People started noticing something bizarre.
Healthy, active rats running around the city
completely missing their tails.
The rat catchers had figured out how to maximize their effort.
Instead of killing their catch, they simply snipped off the tails
and released the rats back into the sewers to breed.
A dead rat pays once. A live rat pays forever.
The most enterprising hunters took this economic logic a step further.
They set up organized commercial rat farms on the outskirts of town
to ensure a steady supply of tails.
When the government finally caught on and halted the payments,
they had purchased a mountain of severed tails.
But the city had a significantly larger rat population
than when the program started.
When humans intervened in a system, the outcomes rarely matched the blueprint.
We see this exact cycle of severe, unintended consequences
repeat relentlessly across modern engineering and technology.
We can track this exact pattern across modern history
by comparing the original design of our tools
against their actual reality.
When telecom engineers developed early SMS,
they built it for a highly restricted purpose,
sending short, one-way alerts from the mobile network directly to subscribers.
The architects didn't anticipate young people hijacking the system.
Teenagers quickly repurposed the alert network,
turning texting into a daily two-way method of personal communication.
Consider GPS. It was constructed exclusively for the military,
engineered to pinpoint global positions and guide naval and aerial navigation.
Today, that military positioning system enables gigaconomy rides and food deliveries.
Even more surprisingly, it's atomic clocks provide the precise timing protocols
that keep our global phone networks, banks, and power grids synchronized and running.
The moment a digital tool or network is released to the public,
it escapes the narrow intentions of its creators.
This resistance to linear planning extends far beyond digital networks.
To protect their sugar cane crops from destructive beetles,
Australia imported cane toads to act as a biological pest control.
The toads barely made a dent in the beetle population.
Instead, they rapidly multiplied, poisoned the native wildlife that tried to eat them,
and aggressively spread across the entire continent.
Look at civil engineering. Houston spent $2.8 billion on a massive project
widening the Katie Freeway, with the strict objective of easing traffic congestion.
This chart shows the actual impact on commute times.
Because all that new road space simply induced demand and encouraged more people to drive,
rush hour trips actually grew 30 to 55 percent longer between 2011 and 2014.
Whether we try to steer biological ecosystems or massive urban traffic grids,
complex systems consistently shatter simple human protections.
Right now, we are deploying a massive new capability and waiting to see how it collides
with reality, artificial intelligence.
Given the historical track record, the firm forecasts we hear from both AI optimists
and AI warriors are almost certainly going to miss the mark.
The most profound impact this technology has during our lifetimes,
whether positive or negative, will likely be an outcome that no researcher,
lab or academic has even conceived of yet.
Faced with this absolute uncertainty, our most effective response is vigilant observation.
We have a compelling mandate to watch how these systems actually behave
once they leave the laboratory and enter the wild.
The most monumental shifts rarely arrive according to a blueprint.
Some of the biggest results are the ones nobody predicted.
And that is the best reason to stay curious.
